title: THEY CAST OUT DEMONS IN JESUS’ NAME… SO WHY DID JESUS SAY, “I NEVER KNEW YOU”?
paragraphs: THEY CAST OUT DEMONS IN JESUS’ NAME… SO WHY DID JESUS SAY, “I NEVER KNEW YOU”?

The terrifying warning of Matthew 7:21–23 isn't about people who rejected Jesus openly. It's about people who called Him Lord, claimed to perform miracles in His name, and believed they belonged to Him—until the moment they heard words no soul would ever want to hear.
Imagine standing before Jesus Christ.
Not in a church service. Not during an altar call. Not while worship music plays and everyone around you has their hands raised.
But before the King Himself.

The One whose eyes see beyond every religious performance. The One who knows what you did when nobody was watching. The One who knows every secret you buried beneath a smile, every prayer you whispered through tears, every sin you justified, and every moment you chose either to surrender or to walk away.
And you are confident.
You remember the ministry you served in. The prayers you prayed. The people you helped. The demons you commanded to leave. The miracles you witnessed. The times you spoke His name with authority.
You have evidence.
You have stories.
You have spiritual accomplishments that would impress an entire congregation.
Then Jesus looks at you.
And instead of welcoming you, He says something that shatters every assumption you ever made about your relationship with God.
“I never knew you: depart from me, ye that work iniquity.” — Matthew 7:23, KJV
Not, “I knew you once.”
Not, “You were Mine until you made one terrible mistake.”
Not, “You failed to perform enough miracles.”
“I never knew you.”
How can someone speak the name of Jesus, perform extraordinary works, and still be rejected by Him?
And perhaps the question that should trouble us even more is this:
Could someone spend an entire lifetime doing things for Jesus without ever truly belonging to Jesus?
Because what Christ reveals in this passage is not merely a warning to false prophets somewhere out there.
It is a warning that reaches into the human heart.
Including yours.
Including mine.
And if we misunderstand it, we may spend our lives measuring spiritual success by things Jesus never promised would prove that we knew Him.
Jesus spoke these words near the conclusion of the Sermon on the Mount.

He had already exposed the danger of religious hypocrisy. He had warned against practicing righteousness merely to be noticed by others. He had taught His listeners that genuine obedience reaches deeper than outward appearances, into anger, lust, truthfulness, mercy, forgiveness, and the secret motives of the heart.
Then came this astonishing declaration:
“Not every one that saith unto me, Lord, Lord, shall enter into the kingdom of heaven; but he that doeth the will of my Father which is in heaven.” — Matthew 7:21, KJV
Notice what Jesus did not say.
He did not say that everyone who uses His name belongs to Him.
He did not say that religious enthusiasm guarantees salvation.
He did not say that spiritual activity automatically proves spiritual life.
He said that not everyone who calls Him Lord will enter the kingdom.
And then He revealed what some of those people would say.
“Lord, Lord, have we not prophesied in thy name? and in thy name have cast out devils? and in thy name done many wonderful works?” — Matthew 7:22, KJV
Read that again.
These are not people presenting a lifetime of atheism as their defense.
They are appealing to religious accomplishments.
They are saying, in effect, “Jesus, look at everything we did in Your name.”
And the frightening part is that they seem genuinely surprised by His response.
They expected recognition.
They received rejection.
They expected their works to establish their relationship with Him.
Jesus exposed the absence of that relationship.
But to understand why, we need to look carefully at what the Scripture actually says.
In the original Greek of Matthew 7:23, Jesus declares:
“Οὐδέποτε ἔγνων ὑμᾶς.”
Transliterated: Oudépote égnōn hymâs.
The meaning is:
“I never knew you.”
The Greek word οὐδέποτε (oudepote) means “never” or “not ever.”
The verb ἔγνων (egnōn) comes from γινώσκω (ginōskō), meaning “to know.”
But here is something important.
Jesus is not saying He lacked information about these people.
That would contradict the biblical testimony concerning His knowledge of human hearts.
John 2:24–25 tells us that Jesus knew what was in humanity. Hebrews 4:13 declares that no creature is hidden from God's sight.
So when Jesus says, “I never knew you,” He is not confessing ignorance.
He is denying that they ever belonged to Him in the saving relationship they claimed.
This is the language of recognition, belonging, and relationship—not merely the possession of information.
Paul gives us a remarkable parallel:
“But if any man love God, the same is known of him.” — 1 Corinthians 8:3, KJV
And again:
“The Lord knoweth them that are his.” — 2 Timothy 2:19, KJV
The issue is not whether Jesus knows that a person exists.
The issue is whether that person is truly His.
That distinction changes everything.
Because you can know biblical facts without knowing Christ.
You can memorize sermons without surrendering your heart.
You can recognize the sound of worship music without worshiping God in spirit and truth.
You can become familiar with Christian language while remaining a stranger to Christian repentance.
And you can learn how to impress religious people without ever being transformed by the grace of Jesus Christ.
There is a difference between being recognized by a congregation and being known by the Savior.
A difference between having a ministry and having genuine fellowship with Christ.
A difference between carrying His name publicly and submitting to His lordship privately.
And Jesus knows the difference.
Perhaps that is why this passage feels so uncomfortable.
Because many of us have learned to evaluate our spiritual condition by visible things.
We ask whether we attend church.
Whether we serve.
Whether we give.
Whether people respect our faith.
Whether our prayers sound powerful.
Whether our posts receive encouragement.
Whether others consider us spiritually mature.
Those things may have value in their proper place.
But none of them can substitute for saving faith in Jesus Christ.
A person can become highly skilled at Christian activity while remaining deeply resistant to Christ Himself.
And that resistance does not always look like open rebellion.
Sometimes it looks like a person who can quote Scripture but refuses to forgive.
A worship leader who sings about surrender but secretly treasures an unrepentant life.
A preacher who speaks passionately about holiness while exploiting the people who trust him.
A believer who publicly defends biblical truth but privately refuses to let that truth confront his own pride.
A person who loves being associated with Jesus but resents being corrected by Jesus.
And before we point toward someone else, we should remember how easily the human heart deceives itself.
We can become experts at identifying hypocrisy in others while explaining away our own.
We can condemn another person's visible sins while protecting the hidden sins that have become comfortable to us.
We can mistake emotional experiences for spiritual maturity.
We can confuse being busy in ministry with being close to God.
And sometimes the most dangerous spiritual condition is not knowing that we are spiritually empty.
It is being convinced that we are full.
But there is another question that demands an answer.
Were these people actually performing miracles?
Jesus says they will claim to have prophesied, cast out demons, and performed mighty works in His name.
The passage records their claims, but it does not explicitly verify that every claimed miracle genuinely occurred.
That distinction matters.
We should not build a doctrine on an assumption Jesus did not state.
Nevertheless, Scripture makes something equally sobering clear: extraordinary spiritual phenomena are not, by themselves, conclusive proof that a person is approved by God.
Consider Judas Iscariot.
Jesus chose twelve apostles and sent them out with authority over unclean spirits and diseases, as Matthew 10:1–8 records.
Judas was among the Twelve, according to Matthew 10:4.
Yet Judas later betrayed Christ.
The text does not tell us whether Judas personally performed a particular miracle during that mission. We should not pretend it does.
But his inclusion among those commissioned with spiritual authority reminds us that participation in extraordinary ministry does not, by itself, establish the final condition of someone's heart.
Or consider the warning Jesus gave in Matthew 24:24:
“For there shall arise false Christs, and false prophets, and shall shew great signs and wonders; insomuch that, if it were possible, they shall deceive the very elect.” — KJV
Signs can be misused to deceive.
Claims of supernatural power can become instruments of manipulation.
And even when God genuinely works through a situation, the person involved cannot claim that divine power as personal proof of holiness.
The power belongs to God.
The glory belongs to God.
The authority belongs to Jesus Christ.
No preacher owns a miracle.
No ministry owns the Holy Spirit.
No spiritual leader becomes exempt from repentance because people admire the results of his work.
That is why Jesus directs our attention away from spectacular accomplishments and toward something far more searching.
He says:
“Depart from me, ye that work iniquity.”
The Greek expression is:
“οἱ ἐργαζόμενοι τὴν ἀνομίαν”
Transliterated: hoi ergazómenoi tēn anomían.
It describes those who practice or work lawlessness.
The word ἀνομία (anomia) refers to lawlessness, wrongdoing, or disregard for God's law.
And the wording portrays people characterized by such practice.
Jesus is not describing someone who hates their sin, falls into temptation, confesses, repents, and returns to Him seeking mercy.
He is exposing people whose religious claims coexist with a life fundamentally opposed to God's will.
They invoke His authority while disregarding His commands.
They appeal to His name while refusing His rule.
They present their accomplishments as a defense while the reality of their lives testifies against them.
And here is where we must be especially careful.
Jesus is not teaching that salvation must be earned through perfect obedience.
That would contradict the Gospel.
Ephesians 2:8–9 declares:
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.” — KJV
We are not saved because we have performed enough good deeds.
We are not accepted because we have accumulated enough religious accomplishments.
We are not forgiven because our obedience has made us worthy of heaven.
We are saved by God's grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
But the same passage continues:
“For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them.” — Ephesians 2:10, KJV
Do you see the distinction?
Good works are not the purchase price of salvation.
They are the fruit of God's transforming grace.
Obedience does not replace faith.
Genuine faith produces a changed relationship with obedience.

The person who belongs to Christ may still struggle, stumble, and grieve over sin. But that person cannot peacefully make rebellion against Christ the settled foundation of life while treating His lordship as meaningless.
The Gospel does not promise that true believers become sinless in this life.
It promises that those who belong to Christ are no longer abandoned to sin as their master.
And when they fall, they have an Advocate.
“And if any man sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous.” — 1 John 2:1, KJV
That verse matters enormously.
Because someone reading this right now may already be frightened.
You may be remembering the addiction you have battled.
The angry words you spoke yesterday.
The temptation you surrendered to after promising yourself you never would again.
The secret struggle you have been too ashamed to tell anyone about.
You may be thinking, “What if Jesus says those words to me?”
Listen carefully.
The purpose of Matthew 7 is not to persuade every struggling Christian that Christ has abandoned them.
It is to destroy false confidence in religious performance and direct us toward the reality of belonging to Him.
There is a profound difference between a person who clings to sin and refuses Christ's correction, and a person who is broken over sin and comes to Christ for mercy.
Not because tears earn salvation.
Not because remorse can wash away guilt.
But because Jesus Christ is a merciful Savior who calls sinners to repentance and promises forgiveness to those who come to Him.
He said:
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.” — John 6:37, KJV
Read those words slowly.
I will in no wise cast out.
The same Jesus who warns of final rejection also promises to receive those who truly come to Him.
We must never silence either truth.
His warnings are real.
His mercy is real.
His holiness is real.
His grace is real.
And the cross is where we see just how seriously God takes both sin and salvation.
Think about the thief crucified beside Jesus.
He had no ministry résumé.
No recorded miracles.
No opportunity to build a Christian organization.
No years left to demonstrate a public record of religious achievement.
He could not descend from his cross to perform acts of service that would impress the crowd.
He could only turn to the crucified Savior and plead:
“Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom.” — Luke 23:42, KJV
And Jesus answered:
“Verily I say unto thee, To day shalt thou be with me in paradise.” — Luke 23:43, KJV
Consider the contrast.
In Matthew 7, people appeal to impressive works performed in Jesus' name.
At Calvary, a dying criminal appeals to Jesus Himself.
One scene exposes the emptiness of trusting in religious accomplishments.
The other displays the sufficiency of Christ's mercy toward a repentant sinner.
The thief had nothing to offer as payment.
But he had turned to the One who was paying the price.
And that is the heart of the Gospel.
We do not enter heaven because we have made ourselves impressive.
We enter through the saving work of Jesus Christ.
He lived in perfect obedience where we have failed.
He bore the penalty of sin through His sacrificial death.
He rose from the dead.
And He calls sinners to repent and believe the Gospel.
This is not cheap grace.
It is costly grace, purchased through the blood of the Son of God and freely received by those who trust Him.
That grace does not leave a person boasting about how much they have accomplished.
It teaches them to boast in the Lord.
It does not make repentance unnecessary.
It makes repentance possible.
It does not make obedience irrelevant.
It gives obedience a new foundation: love for the Savior who first loved us.
And this brings us to something deeply personal.
What if you removed every religious title from your life today?
No pastor.
No worship leader.
No evangelist.
No ministry founder.
No church volunteer.
No Bible teacher.
No Christian content creator.
No audience.
No reputation.
No public applause.
Just you.
Standing before Jesus.
Would you still have a Savior to trust?
Would you still love Him if nobody knew how much you served?
Would you still seek Him if there were no spiritual achievements to display?
Would you still obey when obedience cost you something?
Would you still confess when confession made you look weak?
Would you still believe His grace was enough when all you could bring was your need for mercy?
Because there is a kind of religion that thrives under public attention but withers in private surrender.
And there is a genuine faith that may never become famous on earth but is precious before God.
A mother quietly praying for her wandering child.
A young man resisting temptation when nobody would ever discover his compromise.
A woman learning to forgive someone who deeply wounded her.
A former addict turning again to Christ after another painful battle.
A believer opening Scripture in the middle of the night, desperate to hear truth louder than fear.
An exhausted Christian whispering, “Lord, help my unbelief.”
These are not necessarily the things that attract a crowd.
But God sees what crowds cannot.
And He is not confused about the difference between religious theater and a heart turning toward Him.
Still, we must not turn even these quiet acts into another checklist for earning acceptance.
The foundation remains Christ.
Always Christ.
Our hope is not that we have loved Him flawlessly.
Our hope is that He is a perfect Savior.
Our confidence is not that we have never stumbled.
Our confidence is that His blood is sufficient to cleanse repentant sinners.
Our assurance does not rest on how convincingly we can describe our spiritual experiences.
It rests on the promises of God and the finished work of His Son, whose grace produces the fruit of a changed life.
And perhaps now you can understand why Jesus gave this warning before the final illustration of the Sermon on the Mount.
He immediately spoke about two builders.
One built his house upon rock.
The other built upon sand.
Both had houses.
Both encountered storms.
From a distance, both structures may have appeared secure.
But the storm revealed what appearances concealed.
Jesus identified the wise builder as the person who hears His words and does them.
The foolish builder hears His words but does not act upon them.
And when the storm came, the house built on sand fell.
“And great was the fall of it.” — Matthew 7:27, KJV
That is not an accidental conclusion.
Jesus is showing that hearing His words without responding in obedient faith is a disastrous foundation.
A religious appearance cannot withstand the final judgment.
A spiritual reputation cannot replace reconciliation with God.
And the name of Jesus must never become a decoration placed over a life that refuses Jesus Himself.
Maybe you have spent years building a beautiful-looking house.
You know the songs.
You know the language.
You know when to say “Amen.”
You know how to sound spiritually strong.
People come to you for advice.
They assume you are close to God.
But beneath everything, you know there are rooms in your heart you have refused to open to Him.
Not because He cannot see them.
But because you do not want to surrender what is inside.
Perhaps it is pride.
Perhaps bitterness.
Perhaps a hidden relationship.
Perhaps dishonesty.
Perhaps the desire to be admired more than the desire to be holy.
Perhaps you have learned to use Christian activity to avoid confronting the very things Christ is calling you to repent of.
And the most loving thing anyone could tell you is not that your spiritual résumé looks impressive.
It is that Jesus Christ is worth more than the life you are trying to protect from Him.
You do not need another religious mask.
You need the Savior.
You do not need to manufacture a dramatic testimony.
You need to come into the light.
You do not need to prove that you deserve forgiveness.
You need to repent and trust the One who died and rose again to save sinners.
And if you already belong to Christ but have grown cold, distracted, or spiritually exhausted, His warning can call you back to a life of honest fellowship with Him.
Not toward despair.
Toward repentance.
Not toward self-salvation.
Toward deeper dependence on grace.
Not toward pretending you never struggle.
Toward walking in the light.
Because the Christian life is not a competition to appear the least broken.
It is a life of being redeemed and transformed by Jesus Christ.
That is not merely a beautiful phrase.
It is the testimony of the Gospel.
Peter denied Jesus three times.
He failed publicly and painfully.
Yet the risen Christ restored him, as John 21 records.
Paul once persecuted the church.
Yet the grace of God transformed him into a servant of the very Gospel he had opposed.
The Corinthian believers had come from lives marked by serious sin.
Yet Paul reminded them:
“But ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Spirit of our God.” — 1 Corinthians 6:11, KJV
Their past did not become righteous.
Their sin did not become harmless.
Their stories were changed because Christ had acted in grace.
And He is still the same Savior.
The question is not whether your past is too scandalous.
The question is whether you will come to the One who can forgive and transform you.
The question is not whether your ministry looks successful.
The question is whether your hope rests in Jesus.
The question is not whether you have ever failed Him.
The question is whether you are trusting Him, responding to His Word, and turning from the sin that would draw your heart away.
Because there is one more detail in Matthew 7 that should remain with us long after we finish reading.
Those people said:
“Lord, Lord.”
Twice.
There was urgency in their appeal.
But repeating the right title did not establish the reality of their relationship with Him.
Jesus had already asked in Luke 6:46:
“And why call ye me, Lord, Lord, and do not the things which I say?” — KJV
That question is devastating because it is so simple.
If He is Lord, why do we treat His words as optional?
If He is Savior, why do we seek salvation in our accomplishments?
If He is holy, why do we excuse what He calls sin?
If He is gracious, why do we hide from the very mercy we desperately need?
And if He is worthy of our lives, why are we so willing to give Him our religious appearance while keeping our hearts for ourselves?
These are not questions to answer for the person sitting beside you at church.
They are questions to bring before God.
Tonight, when the noise becomes quiet and there is nobody left to impress, consider praying something like this:

“Lord Jesus, I do not want to hide behind religious activity. Search my heart. Expose what I have refused to surrender. Forgive my sins. Rescue me from trusting in my own works. Teach me to trust Your finished work, love Your truth, and follow You sincerely. Where I have become proud, humble me. Where I have become cold, renew me. Where I have been disobedient, lead me to repentance. I do not want merely to be associated with Your name. I want to belong to You. Have mercy on me, Lord. Amen.”
And please understand something.
The prayer itself is not a magical formula.
Salvation is not produced by repeating particular words.
The invitation of the Gospel is to repent and believe in Jesus Christ.
To turn to Him as the crucified and risen Savior.
To trust His mercy rather than your merit.
To receive His grace rather than attempt to purchase His approval.
And to follow Him as Lord.
If this message has exposed something you have been hiding, you do not have to publish the details of your struggle for strangers to see.
But perhaps you can take one honest step today.
You do not need to explain everything.
God already knows.
And there may be another believer reading your words who can remind you of His promises.
Not as a spiritual trophy.
For the day you become more concerned about people's opinions than God's Word.
For the day you need to remember that the answer to spiritual emptiness is not another performance.
It is returning to Jesus.
Somewhere in your circle of friends may be someone who has quietly mistaken church attendance for salvation.
Someone who has been wounded by religious hypocrisy.
Someone who has abandoned hope because they believe their sins are too great.
Someone who desperately needs to understand both the seriousness of Christ's warning and the greatness of His mercy.
And if you believe this kind of Scripture-centered message deserves to keep reaching people, I want to invite you into something deeper than simply reading another article.
Not because a monthly payment makes anyone more spiritual.
And certainly not because financial support can replace the worship, obedience, generosity, and love that God calls us to offer Him.
But because Christian discipleship matters, biblical teaching matters, and making the Gospel accessible to more people requires faithful effort and practical resources.

Scripture teaches that those who proclaim the Gospel may receive material support for their work (1 Corinthians 9:14), while also teaching that giving should be willing, not pressured or reluctant (2 Corinthians 9:7).
These resources are intended to help you move beyond momentary inspiration into sustained engagement with Scripture, prayer, repentance, spiritual growth, and faithful Christian living.
It is the opportunity to help make Christ-centered truth available to more people.
A young believer learning how to read the Bible.
A father searching for words to pray with his family.
A wounded Christian trying to rebuild trust in God after spiritual disappointment.
A seeker discovering that the Gospel is not a message about becoming impressive enough for heaven, but about the grace of Jesus Christ.
Because this is bigger than growing an audience.
It is about pointing people toward the Savior.
And now, before you leave, return with me to the scene where we began.
A person standing before Jesus.
A lifetime of religious accomplishments.
An appeal filled with confidence.
“Lord, Lord, have we not…?”
There is something heartbreaking about those words.
But there is also something profoundly merciful about Jesus warning us now.
He did not conceal the danger.
He told us.
He placed this warning in Scripture so that we would not mistake religious appearances for saving faith.
He exposed the false foundation while there is still time to hear His words and respond.
And He directs us not toward despairing self-examination without end, but toward Himself—the One who saves sinners by grace, calls them to repentance, and teaches them to walk in His ways.
So do not walk away from this passage merely afraid of hearing “I never knew you.”
Walk away determined not to trust in anything other than the Lord Jesus Christ for your salvation.
Do not make miracles your confidence.
Do not make ministry your righteousness.
Do not make popularity your assurance.
Do not make your past your identity.
Come to Christ.
Trust Christ.
Abide in Christ.
And let the grace that saves you also teach you how to live.

Because on the day when every mask falls away, every title becomes meaningless, and every human achievement is seen for what it truly is, the only Savior sufficient to carry a sinner through judgment will still be Jesus Christ.
The greatest tragedy would not be reaching heaven without a list of miracles to your name. It would be spending your life using the name of Jesus while never coming to Jesus Himself.
